dharana.numbering_edition: Jaideva Singh 1979 (dhāraṇā 1 = verse 24; dhāraṇā 82 = verses 105–106 and dhāraṇā 89 = verses 113–114, otherwise one verse each; dhāraṇā 112 = verse 137)
dharana.sanskrit_iast: vāyudvayasya saṃghaṭṭād antar vā bahir antataḥ | yogī samatvavijñānasamudgamanabhājanam ||
dharana.sanskrit_source: GRETIL e-text, compared with Wallis's concordance, Pradīpaka and the Singh scan
dharana.rendering: From the meeting (saṃghaṭṭa) of the two breaths, within or outside, at its culmination the yogī becomes a vessel for the dawning of the knowledge of sameness (samatva).
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: by the fusion of prāṇa and apāna, at the centre or at the dvādaśānta, there finally arises a complete cessation of both; meditating on that void, in which neither breath is felt, the experience of equality arises. Wallis renders saṃghaṭṭa as 'dynamic tension' and rates the technique advanced.
dharana.technique_name: The Meeting of the Two Breaths
dharana.instruction: Observe only: read and understand this classical description. It is not practised in class. For practice, use Doors 001 to 003.

verification.notes: Door index = Singh dhāraṇā number, read directly in Singh's own headings and cross-checked against The Mystery Within's Singh-numbered list and Wallis's concordance. Caveat: Singh was read from an OCR scan, not a print copy in hand.

numbering_variants.wallis_yukti: verse 64: Fusion of inhalation and exhalation (Y36 ~ A3)

source_disagreements: saṃghaṭṭa: Singh reads 'fusion' leading to complete cessation of both breaths; Wallis reads 'dynamic tension' of the two prāṇas; Bäumer 'meeting'.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 64 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

points: their meeting point: the centre or the dvādaśānta (commentarial)
geometry.summary: Not a body shape. The classical map is the two breath-currents meeting and stilling, inside or outside. Drawn faint: studied, not drilled.
geometry.svg_hint: two arrows meeting head-on at a point, drawn faint to signal observe-only
geometry.honesty: Geometry records the dharana's own map of attention, not a body shape. Locations marked 'commentarial' come from commentary, not from the verse.

reaction.name: Meeting (described)
reaction.summary: School metaphor only: two opposite movements meet and balance. A picture to understand, not an exercise. Not a biochemical or medical claim.

breath.lands_in: wherever the breath naturally ends; this door places nothing on the breath
breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

orientation.cue: Study the verse; let the body simply rest while you do
orientation.gravity: Let the floor or chair carry the body completely; there is no posture to hold
orientation.degrees_hint: No angle target: the VBT gives no posture for this dharana

attention.primary: Understanding the verse: when opposites meet and balance, sameness is known
attention.secondary: If sitting with anything, only the natural pauses of Doors 001 to 003

adiyogi.verse_paraphrase: From the meeting (saṃghaṭṭa) of the two breaths, within or outside, at its culmination the yogī becomes a vessel for the dawning of the knowledge of sameness (samatva).
adiyogi.method_summary: Classical method: the in-breath and out-breath are brought to meet, inside or outside, until in Singh's reading both cease; resting in that void, the knowledge of sameness arises. Observe-only in this school: read and understand it. Do not stop the breath. For practice, use Doors 001 to 003.

honesty.disclosure: Door 041 follows Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 41 (verse 64) in Jaideva Singh's numbering. The door-to-dharana index is a School of 112 Doorways teaching device. Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.
honesty.notes: pairing_type is school_device: the dharana is the content, while the door index, seat and pacing are the school's.
flags: Door index = Jaideva Singh dharana number: Door 041 is dharana 41, verse 64. Other editions number differently (see dharana.numbering_variants).
The seat, breath counts, reaction metaphor, attention-map drawing and beat scripts are school devices, not part of the verse.
The English is a school paraphrase, not a quotation from any translator.
No medical claims. Reaction names are metaphors, not biochemistry.
New door researched on 2026-10-06 on branch research/vbt-houses-2-7; awaiting guardian review.

historical/observe_only: In Singh's reading the practice culminates in the complete cessation of in-breath and out-breath; this school does not induce breath cessation. Taught as text to understand, not as a class drill.

safety.pain_rule: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.
safety.open_seat_alternate: This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
safety.contraindication_notes: General practice caution only; not medical advice. Breath cessation is not taught by this school. Never hold or stop the breath for this door. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
safety.observe_only_note: Observe-only. Inducing a stop of the breath can bring dizziness or fainting and is not suitable for everyone, for example during pregnancy or with heart, blood-pressure or breathing conditions. For practice, use the natural-pause forms of Doors 001 to 003.

beats.title: Name the door
beats.script: This is Door 041: the meeting of the two breaths. Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 41, verse 64. This door is observe-only.

beats.title: Geometry
beats.script: No shape to make, and no drill. Sit comfortably while we read. Its classical map is two breath-currents meeting and stilling.

beats.title: Orientation
beats.script: Let the body rest completely. Eyes open, reading or resting softly. Attention on understanding, not on doing.

beats.title: Breath
beats.script: Natural breath only. Nothing to practise with the breath here. No forced hold.

beats.title: Attention
beats.script: Hold the idea, not the breath: when opposite movements meet and balance, sameness can be known.

beats.title: Reaction cue
beats.script: School image: two currents meeting and balancing. A metaphor, not medicine.

beats.title: Adiyogi thread
beats.script: Verse 64: describes the meeting of the two breaths, inside or outside, and the dawning of the knowledge of sameness. Observe-only here: we do not stop the breath. For practice, use Doors 001 to 003.

beats.title: Exit / integrate
beats.script: Close the text. Take a normal breath. Look around the room and move on when ready.
